Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- UK Prime Minister Gordon Brown has branded the cholera crisis in Zimbabwe "an international emergency" and called on the world community to confront President Robert Mugabe, leader of the central African nation. A shortage of clean drinking water has unleashed a cholera epidemic in Zimbabwe. "This is now an international rather than a national emergency," Brown said in a statement Saturday. "International because disease crosses borders. International because the systems of government in Zimbabwe are now broken. There is no state capable or willing of protecting its people." Earlier this week the government of Zimbabwe, which already suffers from severe economic problems and political instability, declared a national emergency following the outbreak, which has so far killed more than 600 people. Cholera, a water-borne disease, is on the increase in nine of Zimbabwe's 10 provinces, the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned. It blamed "poor water and sanitation supply, a collapsed health system and limited government capacity to respond to the emergency." Many of those afflicted with the disease have fled to neighboring countries to seek medical help -- which risks spreading the outbreak still further. Brown called on the international community to tell Mugabe "enough is enough," and suggested that the United Nations Security Council meet to discuss the issue. He added that the most pressing issue was to ensure that testing and rehydration equipment and packs reach the right people, as well as for aid agencies to set up a organizational structure in the state capital Harare to confront the disease. "The people of Zimbabwe voted for a better future. It is our duty to support that aspiration," Brown added.   Brown's comments came one day after U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said that the outbreak is the latest sign that Mugabe's rule over the country must end. "It's well past time for Robert Mugabe to leave. I think that's now obvious," Rice said during a visit to Denmark. Washington has long called for Mugabe to leave office, with President George W. Bush calling Zimbabwe's runoff presidential election in June a "sham" and instructing Rice and other U.S. officials to develop additional sanctions against Mugabe's "illegitimate government." "The United States will always do anything and everything that it can to help innocent people who are suffering," Rice said. "And we are not going to deny assistance to people in need because of their government. But if this is not evidence to the international community that it's time to stand up for what is right, I don't know what will be. And frankly, the nations of the region have to lead it." Rice -- who has just about a month left in office before President-elect Barack Obama's administration takes over -- also called on all African nations to speak up. Asked whether the United States and Europe should try to force out Mugabe, Rice responded, "Well, without help in the region, it's very difficult to have the tools that will bring about a just resolution in Zimbabwe. The United States and Europe can't do everything alone. Other states are responsible too. And the southern African states should be the most responsible at this point, because they have the most at risk. And the people of Zimbabwe have suffered long enough." Supporters of Mugabe, who has come under heavy international criticism for several years, were accused of political intimidation following June's presidential  runoff vote. For months there have been some efforts to build a power-sharing government between Mugabe's ruling Zanu PF party and the opposition movement for Democratic Change, led by Morgan Tsvangirai, to little avail. On Thursday, Mugabe hinted he may form a Cabinet without the opposition and call for early elections. The opposition responded that it would welcome a "genuine election," with international supervision. The 84-year-old Mugabe, who has led Zimbabwe since its independence in 1980 from Great Britain, also suggested he would ignore an international tribunal ruling that declared illegal his government's seizure of farms from white Zimbabweans.

(CNN) — UK Prime Minister Gordon Brown has described the cholera crisis in Zimbabwe as “an international emergency” and urged the global community to confront President Robert Mugabe, the leader of the central African nation.

A shortage of clean drinking water has triggered a cholera epidemic in Zimbabwe. “This is now an international rather than a national emergency,” Brown said in a statement Saturday. “International because disease crosses borders. International because the systems of government in Zimbabwe are now broken. There is no state capable or willing of protecting its people.”

Earlier this week, Zimbabwe’s government, already grappling with severe economic hardship and political instability, declared a national emergency following the outbreak, which has killed more than 600 people so far.

Cholera, a waterborne disease, is spreading in nine of Zimbabwe’s 10 provinces, the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned. The agency attributed the crisis to “poor water and sanitation supply, a collapsed health system and limited government capacity to respond to the emergency.”

Many people afflicted with the disease have fled to neighboring countries in search of medical treatment, raising the risk that the outbreak could spread even further.

Brown called on the international community to tell Mugabe that “enough is enough” and suggested that the United Nations Security Council convene to discuss the crisis. He added that the most urgent priority was to ensure that testing and rehydration equipment and packs reach those in need, and that aid agencies establish an organizational structure in the state capital, Harare, to combat the disease.

“The people of Zimbabwe voted for a better future. It is our duty to support that aspiration,” Brown added.

Brown’s remarks came one day after U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said the outbreak was the latest indication that Mugabe’s rule must come to an end.

“It’s well past time for Robert Mugabe to leave. I think that’s now obvious,” Rice said during a visit to Denmark.

Washington has long called for Mugabe to step down, with President George W. Bush describing Zimbabwe’s June runoff presidential election as a “sham” and directing Rice and other U.S. officials to develop additional sanctions against Mugabe’s “illegitimate government.”

“The United States will always do anything and everything that it can to help innocent people who are suffering,” Rice said. “And we are not going to deny assistance to people in need because of their government. But if this is not evidence to the international community that it’s time to stand up for what is right, I don’t know what will be. And frankly, the nations of the region have to lead it.”

Rice, who has just about a month left in office before President-elect Barack Obama’s administration takes over, also called on all African nations to speak out.

Asked whether the United States and Europe should try to force Mugabe out, Rice responded: “Well, without help in the region, it’s very difficult to have the tools that will bring about a just resolution in Zimbabwe. The United States and Europe can’t do everything alone. Other states are responsible too. And the southern African states should be the most responsible at this point, because they have the most at risk. And the people of Zimbabwe have suffered long enough.”

Supporters of Mugabe, who has faced heavy international criticism for several years, were accused of political intimidation following June’s presidential runoff vote.

For months, efforts have been underway to build a power-sharing government between Mugabe’s ruling Zanu PF party and the opposition Movement for Democratic Change, led by Morgan Tsvangirai, but with little success.

On Thursday, Mugabe suggested he might form a Cabinet without the opposition and call for early elections. The opposition responded that it would welcome a “genuine election” conducted under international supervision.

The 84-year-old Mugabe, who has led Zimbabwe since its independence from Great Britain in 1980, also suggested he would ignore an international tribunal ruling that declared illegal his government’s seizure of farms from white Zimbabweans.

“This is now an international rather than a national emergency,” Brown said in a statement on Saturday. He said it was international because illnesses spread across borders, and because Zimbabwe’s governing institutions had collapsed. “There is no state capable or willing of protecting its people,” he said.

Earlier in the week, Zimbabwe’s government declared a national emergency over the outbreak. The country was already facing serious economic hardship and political turmoil. More than 600 people have died so far.

The U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, or OCHA, warned that cholera, which is spread through contaminated water, is increasing in nine of Zimbabwe’s 10 provinces. The agency pointed to inadequate water and sanitation services, the breakdown of the health care system, and the government’s limited ability to deal with the crisis.

Many people infected with cholera have crossed into nearby countries in search of treatment, raising fears that the disease could spread even more widely.

Brown urged the global community to tell Mugabe that “enough is enough” and proposed that the United Nations Security Council convene to address the situation. He said the immediate priority was to make sure that testing supplies, rehydration materials, and treatment packs reached those who needed them. He also called for aid organizations to establish a coordinated structure in Harare, Zimbabwe’s capital, to fight the epidemic.

“The people of Zimbabwe voted for a better future. It is our duty to support that aspiration,” Brown said.

Brown’s remarks came a day after U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said the cholera crisis was further proof that Mugabe’s time in power should end.

“It’s well past time for Robert Mugabe to leave. I think that’s now obvious,” Rice said while visiting Denmark.

The United States has long demanded that Mugabe step down. President George W. Bush called Zimbabwe’s June presidential runoff election a “sham” and directed Rice and other American officials to prepare additional sanctions against what he described as Mugabe’s “illegitimate government.”

Rice said the United States would continue to help innocent people who were suffering. “And we are not going to deny assistance to people in need because of their government,” she said. But she added that if the cholera outbreak did not persuade the international community to act, she did not know what would. She said countries in the region, in particular, needed to take the lead.

Rice, who had about one month left in office before President-elect Barack Obama’s administration was due to take over, also urged African nations to speak out.

When asked whether the United States and Europe should attempt to push Mugabe from power, Rice said it would be extremely difficult to achieve a fair outcome in Zimbabwe without support from neighboring countries. She said the United States and Europe could not handle the situation by themselves and that other governments also had obligations. Southern African nations, she said, had the greatest responsibility because they faced the greatest risks. “And the people of Zimbabwe have suffered long enough,” she added.

Mugabe, who has faced strong international condemnation for years, saw his supporters accused of using political intimidation after the June presidential runoff. For months, attempts had been made to create a power-sharing government between Mugabe’s ruling Zanu PF party and the opposition Movement for Democratic Change, led by Morgan Tsvangirai, but little progress had been achieved.

On Thursday, Mugabe indicated that he might appoint a Cabinet without including the opposition and could call early elections. The opposition said it would support a “genuine election” if it were monitored internationally.

Mugabe, 84, has ruled Zimbabwe since the country gained independence from Britain in 1980. He also suggested he would disregard a ruling by an international tribunal that found his government’s seizure of farms from white Zimbabweans to be unlawful.

**LONDON, England (CNN)** — British Prime Minister Gordon Brown has described Zimbabwe’s worsening cholera outbreak as an “international emergency” and called for stronger action against President Robert Mugabe, accusing his government of failing its people amid a deepening humanitarian crisis.

Brown said the spread of the disease, coupled with Zimbabwe’s collapsing health system, food shortages and political turmoil, demanded an urgent international response.

“This is now an international rather than a national emergency,” Brown said, urging the global community to increase pressure on Mugabe’s government and support efforts to deliver medical aid to those affected.

The cholera outbreak has killed hundreds of people and infected thousands more, according to international health officials. Aid agencies say the disease has spread rapidly because of broken water systems, poor sanitation and the near-collapse of public hospitals.

Zimbabwe’s crisis has intensified following months of political deadlock after disputed elections. Mugabe, who has ruled the country since independence in 1980, has faced growing international condemnation over allegations of election violence, economic mismanagement and human rights abuses.

Brown said Mugabe’s leadership had turned a preventable health crisis into a catastrophe.

“The people of Zimbabwe deserve better,” he said, adding that Mugabe should not be allowed to “continue to inflict suffering” on the country.

International aid organizations have warned that the cholera outbreak could spread further without immediate access to clean water, medical supplies and functioning treatment centers. Neighboring countries have also expressed concern as cases have appeared across borders.

Zimbabwean officials have blamed Western sanctions for the country’s economic collapse, but critics say Mugabe’s policies and political repression are responsible for the breakdown of basic services.

Brown called on African leaders and international institutions to intensify diplomatic efforts, saying the crisis was no longer only a Zimbabwean issue but a threat to regional stability.

“This is a humanitarian disaster,” he said. “The world must act.”

**HARARE, Zimbabwe (AP) —** Zimbabwe’s cholera epidemic has deepened into a political and humanitarian crisis, with thousands infected, hospitals overwhelmed and Western leaders accusing President Robert Mugabe’s government of presiding over the collapse of basic public services.

The outbreak, which began in August 2008 and surged late in the year, has spread through densely populated townships and across Zimbabwe’s borders, driven by broken water systems, burst sewage pipes, shortages of medicine and a collapsing health sector. Aid agencies have warned that the disease could continue to spread unless clean water, sanitation and emergency treatment are restored.

British Prime Minister Gordon Brown called the epidemic “an international rather than a national emergency” and said the crisis reflected the failure of Mugabe’s leadership. Brown urged stronger international action to support relief efforts and increase pressure on Zimbabwe’s government, saying ordinary Zimbabweans were paying the price for political paralysis and misrule.

U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice also sharply criticized Mugabe, saying it was “well past time” for him to leave power. Rice said Zimbabwe’s worsening cholera outbreak and economic collapse showed that Mugabe’s rule had become a threat to his own people and the region.

Zimbabwe’s government has blamed Western sanctions and outside interference for the country’s troubles, while critics say years of economic mismanagement, political repression and neglect of infrastructure have left the country unable to contain a preventable disease.

The cholera epidemic unfolded as Zimbabwe remained mired in a political standoff following disputed 2008 elections. Mugabe and opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai had agreed in principle to a power-sharing arrangement, but implementation stalled amid disputes over control of key ministries.

Relief organizations have been expanding cholera treatment centers and distributing water purification tablets, but workers say shortages of staff, fuel, vehicles and supplies have hampered the response. Neighboring South Africa and other countries in the region have also reported cases linked to cross-border movement.

Cholera, an acute diarrheal disease spread through contaminated water or food, can kill within hours if untreated but is usually manageable with oral rehydration salts and intravenous fluids. Health officials say Zimbabwe’s high death toll reflects both the scale of the outbreak and the severe breakdown of the country’s medical system.

counterfactuals.output:
(CNN) -- Zimbabwe’s cholera epidemic has deepened a national crisis already marked by the collapse of public services, soaring hunger and intensifying international calls for President Robert Mugabe to relinquish power.

Health workers and aid agencies say the waterborne disease has spread rapidly through densely populated townships and rural districts where clean water, sanitation and basic medical care have broken down. Hospitals and clinics, long weakened by shortages of medicine, equipment and staff, have struggled to treat patients arriving with severe dehydration. In many communities, residents say they have been forced to draw water from unsafe wells, rivers or burst sewage systems after municipal supplies failed.

The outbreak has become one of the starkest signs of Zimbabwe’s broader state failure. Public hospitals have closed wards or turned patients away because doctors and nurses are absent, unpaid or unable to afford transportation to work. Schools have been disrupted. Garbage collection has stopped in some urban areas. Sewage pipes have burst and gone unrepaired. Inflation has rendered salaries nearly worthless, while food shortages have left millions dependent on relief.

Aid organizations warn that cholera can be contained with swift treatment, clean water and basic sanitation, but Zimbabwe’s crumbling infrastructure has allowed the disease to spread across provincial boundaries and, in some cases, into neighboring countries. The epidemic has also heightened fears that other preventable diseases could surge as the country’s health system deteriorates further.

The humanitarian emergency is unfolding against a tense political backdrop. Mugabe, who has ruled Zimbabwe since independence in 1980, has faced mounting pressure from Western governments, African leaders, church groups and human rights organizations to step down or accept a genuine power-sharing arrangement with the opposition.

Critics accuse Mugabe’s government of presiding over economic ruin, suppressing political opponents and failing to respond adequately to the cholera outbreak. They say the epidemic is not only a medical disaster but also the result of years of mismanagement, corruption and political repression that hollowed out once-functioning public institutions.

Mugabe and his supporters have rejected calls for his resignation, often blaming Zimbabwe’s suffering on Western sanctions and outside interference. The government has previously accused Britain, the United States and other critics of using the crisis to undermine Zimbabwe’s sovereignty. But opposition leaders and civil society groups argue that the government’s explanations do little to address the immediate reality facing Zimbabweans: empty pharmacies, dry taps, broken sewers and families burying relatives lost to a treatable disease.

Regional pressure has also grown. Some African leaders, who for years were reluctant to publicly criticize Mugabe, have voiced alarm over the scale of the humanitarian disaster. Diplomats have warned that Zimbabwe’s collapse threatens regional stability, particularly as desperate citizens cross borders in search of food, medical treatment and work.

The opposition Movement for Democratic Change has said the cholera epidemic demonstrates the urgent need for political change and a functioning government capable of restoring basic services. Efforts to implement a power-sharing deal have been hampered by disputes over control of key ministries, including those overseeing security and home affairs.

Meanwhile, ordinary Zimbabweans continue to bear the consequences. In townships around Harare and other cities, families queue for water, search for scarce medicine and rely on neighbors or aid workers to transport the sick. Funerals have become more frequent in areas where cholera treatment centers are overwhelmed or too far away to reach in time.

Public health specialists say the solution is straightforward in medical terms: rapid rehydration, antibiotics in severe cases, safe drinking water, disinfected sanitation systems and public education. But they warn that none of those measures can be sustained without a functioning state apparatus and unhindered humanitarian access.

International agencies have appealed for expanded emergency assistance, including water-purification tablets, oral rehydration salts, intravenous fluids and support for health clinics. But aid workers say the response must go beyond emergency treatment to address the collapse of the systems that allowed the outbreak to explode.

For many Zimbabweans, the cholera epidemic has become a symbol of a country in free fall — a once-prosperous nation where the most basic public services can no longer be taken for granted. As the death toll rises and diplomatic pressure intensifies, the central political question remains unresolved: whether Mugabe will yield to demands for change, or whether Zimbabwe’s humanitarian crisis will continue to worsen under a paralyzed and contested government.

## Zimbabwe’s Humanitarian and Political Crisis Under Robert Mugabe

Zimbabwe’s crisis under President Robert Mugabe deepened dramatically in 2008, as political paralysis, economic collapse, food shortages and a deadly cholera epidemic converged into one of the country’s worst emergencies since independence.

The cholera outbreak became a stark symbol of the breakdown of basic services. With water systems, sanitation and hospitals failing, the disease spread rapidly through crowded urban areas and impoverished communities. At the time, the reported cholera death toll had risen to more than 500 people, with thousands more infected, while aid agencies warned that the true scale could grow if clean water, medical supplies and functioning clinics were not restored.

The United Nations issued increasingly urgent warnings about Zimbabwe’s humanitarian situation. U.N. officials said millions of Zimbabweans were in need of food aid, while the cholera epidemic threatened to expand further because of collapsed public health infrastructure. The organization and international relief agencies also warned that the crisis was being worsened by political instability and restrictions that complicated aid delivery.

The political crisis stemmed from Mugabe’s disputed hold on power after the 2008 elections. Opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai and his Movement for Democratic Change had challenged Mugabe’s rule, but a violent and contested election process led to a stalled power-sharing agreement. Critics accused Mugabe’s government of using intimidation and state power to cling to office while the country’s economy and institutions disintegrated.

International pressure on Mugabe intensified. British Prime Minister Gordon Brown condemned the Zimbabwean leader’s handling of the crisis, saying that “enough is enough” and calling for Mugabe to go. Brown described the emergency as not only a national failure but an international concern, arguing that Zimbabwe’s leadership had lost legitimacy amid preventable suffering.

U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice also sharply criticized Mugabe, saying it was “well past time” for him to leave power. Rice argued that Mugabe’s rule had devastated Zimbabwe and that the stalled power-sharing process could not be credible while repression and humanitarian collapse continued.

Together, the cholera epidemic, mass hunger, economic ruin and disputed political authority exposed the severity of Zimbabwe’s breakdown under Mugabe. The crisis drew global condemnation and urgent calls for political change, humanitarian access and the restoration of basic public services.

counterfactuals.output:
**LONDON, England (CNN) — December 2008**  

British Prime Minister Gordon Brown declared Zimbabwe’s cholera outbreak an “international emergency” Saturday, intensifying pressure on President Robert Mugabe to step down as the disease spread through a country already crippled by political deadlock, economic collapse and a failing health system.

“This is now an international rather than a national emergency,” Brown said, accusing Mugabe’s government of failing to protect its people and obstructing efforts to address the crisis. Brown said the outbreak exposed the “breakdown” of Zimbabwe’s state institutions and renewed calls for Mugabe to leave power.

“Enough is enough,” Brown said. “Mugabe must go.”

The cholera epidemic has killed hundreds of people and infected thousands more, according to international health officials. Aid agencies say the true toll may be higher because many Zimbabweans are unable to reach clinics or hospitals, many of which lack medicine, clean water and staff.

The outbreak has spread beyond Zimbabwe’s borders, with cases reported in neighboring South Africa and other countries in the region, raising alarm among public health officials and governments across southern Africa.

Cholera, a waterborne disease that can kill within hours if untreated, is usually preventable with clean drinking water and proper sanitation. But Zimbabwe’s water system has deteriorated sharply amid years of economic crisis, hyperinflation and shortages of basic supplies.

Hospitals and clinics have been overwhelmed. Doctors and nurses have gone on strike or stopped reporting to work because their wages have become nearly worthless. In some areas, residents have been forced to draw water from contaminated wells and rivers.

The growing health emergency comes months after a disputed presidential election plunged Zimbabwe into a prolonged political crisis. Opposition leader Morgan Tsvangirai, who won the first round of voting in March, withdrew from a June runoff citing violence against his supporters. Mugabe, in power since independence in 1980, proceeded with the runoff and claimed victory.

A power-sharing deal brokered by regional leaders in September has stalled over control of key ministries, including home affairs, leaving the country without an effective unity government as conditions worsen.

International criticism of Mugabe has mounted in recent days. U.S. and European officials have accused him of clinging to power while Zimbabweans suffer, and some African leaders have also begun to openly question his rule — a notable shift in a region where criticism of Mugabe has often been muted.

Mugabe’s government has rejected outside pressure, blaming Western sanctions for the country’s collapse and accusing Britain and its allies of using the cholera outbreak to justify intervention.

Aid organizations say politics must not be allowed to delay the emergency response. The United Nations and humanitarian groups have appealed for medical supplies, water-treatment chemicals and greater access to affected communities.

Brown said Britain would increase assistance through international agencies but insisted that Zimbabwe’s suffering could not be separated from its leadership crisis.

“The tragedy is that this is a man-made disaster,” he said. “Zimbabwe’s people need food, medicine and clean water — and they need a government that serves them.”
